newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO renews peace mission in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: NATO renews peace mission in Bosnia.

text.p: NATO commanders on Friday formally launched a new multinational peacekeeping mission in Bosnia to take over from a force that helped end the worst war in Europe since Word War Two.

NATO's supreme commander in Europe, General George Joulwan, presided over a military ceremony handing over authority to the 35,000-strong Stabilisation Force (SFOR), which succeeds the much bigger NATO-led Implementation Force (IFOR).
Joulwan said in a speech the new force would work to solidify the fragile peace that has held since the signing of the Dayton peace accords in December 1995.
"IFOR has provided the wind of opportunity and SFOR will provide the stable environment for the transition of your country from war to peace," Joulwan said.
Ultimately it was Bosnia's political leaders who would determine whether the peace would last, he said.
"It is up to you. You must take risks for peace as our soldiers have taken risks," he said. "You and only you can create a better Bosnia-Herzegovina for your children and grandchildren."
The NATO general paid tribute to soldiers who had died during the Bosnia mission. "They served a noble cause. They did make a differernce, their sacrifices were not in vain."
With hundreds of soldiers standing at attention under wintry grey skies, Joulwan officially "activated" SFOR and told the troops: "Let's get on with it".
U.S. General William Crouch, the commander of SFOR, will be working with about half the number of troops than the previous IFOR contingent, which had close to 60,000 at its height.
Apart from the new acronym and the scaled-down size, the NATO-led mission remains essentially the same.
Western countries are anxious to cut down on their expensive military commitment in Bosnia and the new force allows them to begin to do that.
NATO ministers in Brussels are due to review the mission's status every six months.
The leading armies in the peace force, the United States, Britain and France, have already reduced the number of troops serving in the force in keeping with the SFOR mandate.
The United States has offered 8,000 troops for the new force, about half the number of soldiers it deployed for IFOR.
Some 2,000 German combat troops are due to arrive in January, the first such deployment since World War Two.
SFOR also includes a Russian contingent, which agreed to renew its participation, along with soldiers from 16 other non- NATO countries.
Military analysts, diplomats and Bosnian leaders agree that the country could easily plunge back into warfare without a strong NATO presence.
Over the past year, NATO-led troops have successfully enforced the military terms of the Dayton accords, separating Bosnia's rival armies and overseeing the storage of heavy weapons.
The civilian side of the treaty has been stalled, with Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders locked in disputes that have hampered efforts at building a post-war government and economic reconstruction.
NATO officers say privately that some sort of a multinational force will have to stay in Bosnia well beyond the expiry of SFOR's 18-month mandate.
